text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementHealthRethinking the Mechanisms of Alzheimer’s DiseaseAlzheimer’s disease is the most common form of dementia, but memory isn’t the only thing it affectsRLBy Rémi Lamontagne-Caron11:00 AM CDT on September 10, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleAlzheimer’s disease is the most common form of dementia. For many years, researchers believed that its main cause was a buildup of toxic proteins. But recent findings suggest that the problem may have another origin, specifically in the bloodstream.Subscribe to skip adsFeatured VideoPowered By 10 Dogs Might Be Blinking as a Way to Communicate With You: StudyShareNextStayContrary to a commonly held belief, dementia isn’t just about memory. Imagine the brain as a car. To run properly, this complex system depends, among other things, on an engine (our neurons, the central component) and a set of pipes (our cerebral vascular system) to deliver fuel (oxygen and nutrients) to the engine.As we age, this machinery wears out. If the pipes become damaged, rust sets in. If the engine breaks down, it affects the vehicle’s performance and inevitably leads to premature failure. In the case of Alzheimer’s disease, the “rust” is characterized by the accumulation of two toxic proteins: amyloid plaques and tau fibres, which bring about a decline in cognitive abilities, including memory.Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
